items.title: Filling the empty vessel: How the Supreme Court now attributes mens rea to companies
items.summary: Corporate criminal liability has always sat awkwardly with the basic idea of a guilty mind. A company, in the old line, has "no soul to damn and no body to kick." It can't form intent the way a person does. Still, companies hold enormous economic power and can-do real harm, so legal systems have had to find ways to make them answer for crimes. In India, the Supreme Court settled in Iridium India Telecom Ltd. v. Motorola Inc. , (2011) 1 SCC 74 , that a company can have mens rea . What it never explained was how : through whom, and on what basis. As the Court put it in Sanofi , that question remained "an empty vessel, yet to be filled." On September 7, 2026, the Court finally filled it with a three-stage framework, built after a careful look at English law from Lennard's Carrying through to the reforms that followed Barclays . This is the first time the Supreme Court has set out a complete doctrinal basis for attributing mens rea to a company. It will change how corporate prosecutions are brought, defended and decided. items.title: ECI’s reforms cannot erase past failures
items.summary: Imagine you're a patient in a hospital and the hospital tells you: “From tomorrow, we’ll maintain proper records of every important decision about your treatment. We’ll make sure doctors can make the decisions without being overridden by a computer system. And if something goes wrong, we’ll investigate what happened.” You are not going to say, “Waah - Great reforms.” You would ask: “Hello, Wait. What was happening till yesterday?” That is exactly where we need to begin with the Election Commission of India. After months of questions over its functioning, the ECI has suddenly announced a series of changes: agendas will be circulated, minutes recorded, IT systems screened, and some SIR-affected voters given additional assistance. But these aren't just changes for tomorrow. They raise questions about what happened yesterday: what procedures were followed, who made the decisions, and who authorised them? Let Me Explain.
